identity.title: rStar-Math: Small LLMs Can Master Math Reasoning with Self-Evolved Deep Thinking

problem.claim: Can small language models achieve strong mathematical reasoning through self-evolved test-time search, without distillation from superior models?

contributions.claim: rStar-Math combines MCTS test-time search, an SLM math policy, and an SLM-based process reward model.
It introduces code-augmented CoT synthesis with verified trajectories, process reward-model training without naive step-level score annotation, and iterative self-evolution of both SLMs.
The authors report releasing code and data.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish rStar-Math by its three innovations: code-augmented MCTS reasoning-data synthesis, process reward-model training that avoids naive step-level annotation, and from-scratch iterative self-evolution.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that four self-evolution rounds using millions of synthesized solutions for 747k math problems brought SLMs to state-of-the-art levels.
The authors report improving Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH from 58.8% to 90.0%, surpassing o1-preview by a stated +4.5%, whose relative-versus-percentage-point interpretation is unspecified.
The authors report solving an average of 53.3% (8/15) of AIME problems and describe this as among the top 20% of the brightest high-school math students; the comparison basis is unspecified.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper presents rStar-Math to test whether small language models can rival or surpass OpenAI o1 without distillation from stronger models.
It uses MCTS-guided deep thinking with a policy SLM and process reward model, supported by code-augmented verified reasoning synthesis.
The policy SLM and process reward model are built from scratch and iteratively evolved across four rounds using large-scale synthesized solutions.
The authors report large MATH gains and an AIME result framed as comparable to performance among top high-school students.
Code and data are reported as publicly available.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a distinctive mechanism—MCTS guided by an SLM process reward model—with concrete benchmark deltas and problem counts.

lessons.interpretation: A mechanism-to-evidence pairing makes it easier to connect the proposed training recipe with the reported outcome.
lessons.application: When presenting a new reasoning system, name the search or training mechanism alongside dataset scale, iteration count, and benchmark change.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the work is primarily conceptual or lacks quantitative evaluation.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify evaluation protocols, sampling or search budgets, statistical variation, or the precise o1 comparison setup.
The basis and source of the AIME student-ranking comparison are not described.
The abstract does not identify which model sizes or configurations achieved the reported state-of-the-art results.
